lines.text: Every morning, in a classroom you have never been to, a seven year old opens a book.
A few times a year, her teacher sits beside her and listens. And makes a small mark on paper every time a word goes wrong.
It takes a minute to read. It takes four more to score. And there are twenty seven other children waiting.
So we built something that does the counting. It runs on the laptop already sitting on her desk.
And the first thing it does is disconnect.
She reads. The words arrive on the screen, and every one is measured against the page she was handed.
Green, she read it. Red, she did not. And amber, where the machine is not sure enough to call it a mistake. So it doesn't.
Her teacher can overrule any of it, in either direction. She is the one doing the assessing. We only hold the stopwatch.
We built one more thing. A layer that refuses to mark a child down for the way their family speaks.
Then we measured whether it ever worked.
The speech model had already rewritten her voice into standard spelling, long before our rules could see it. So we published the zero, and the reason for it.
What we found underneath was bigger. On the speech it was meant to protect, the recogniser pulls words apart and fuses them together. No rule about pronunciation can reach that.
On a clean read, we tell a child they made a mistake four times in every thousand words. That is the number we care about most.
Because telling a child who read it perfectly that she got it wrong is the worse thing to be.
No subscription. No account. No child's voice ever leaving the room.
